references.text: The parallel text in Mark describes the same event where the possessed man falls down before Jesus and cries out: "What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?" and begs him not to torment him.
The parallel text in Matthew about the demon-possessed men in Gadara who cry out "What have we to do with you, Son of God?" and ask if Jesus has come to torment them before the appointed time.

In the synagogue at Capernaum, an unclean spirit cries out: "What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God!" – the demons recognize Jesus' identity and express fear.
Luke's account of the unclean spirit in the synagogue at Capernaum crying out "What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth?" – the same pattern where demons identify Jesus and fear his power.
The angel Gabriel announces that Jesus will be called "Son of the Most High" (υἱὸς ὑψίστου), the same title used by the demon here.
James writes that even demons believe God is one – and they shudder. This shows that demons have knowledge of God, consistent with the demon here recognizing Jesus as Son of the Most High God.
Melchizedek blesses Abram in the name of God Most High (El Elyon). The title "God Most High" has roots in the Old Testament and is used here by the demon to refer to Jesus' Father.
Balaam speaks of the knowledge of the Most High (Elyon) – an Old Testament use of the title that the demon in Luke 8:28 applies to God.
The psalmist praises the Lord as the Most High (Elyon) over all the earth. The demon's confession of Jesus as "Son of the Most High God" links him to this Old Testament divine title.
Revelation's description of the devil's final torment (basanismos) – the Greek word βασανίσῃς in Luke 8:28 points to the demons' fear of final judgment and punishment.
Peter writes about angels who sinned and were cast into dark dungeons to be held for judgment – this sheds light on the demons' fear of being tormented, as expressed in Luke 8:28.
